The central question is whether a model's confidence scores remain well-calibrated — i.e., whether a stated 85% confidence actually corresponds to ~85% empirical accuracy — when the deployment distribution differs from training, and specifically whether the degree of that miscalibration is predictable from properties of pre-training. The key concepts in tension are: calibration (alignment between predicted probability and empirical frequency), distribution shift (the gap between training and test marginals), pre-training data mixture entropy (how diverse or concentrated the sources were across domains, languages, and formats), and task specificity (whether the downstream task is narrow and well-defined versus broad and compositional). An expert immediately worries about a confound beginners miss entirely: calibration metrics like ECE (Expected Calibration Error) are themselves distribution-dependent, so a model can appear well-calibrated on a held-out set while being systematically overconfident on the specific slice of that set that corresponds to genuine out-of-distribution inputs — the aggregate metric papers over catastrophic local failure. The deeper concern is directional asymmetry: high-entropy pre-training mixtures may improve average calibration under mild shift but can increase overconfidence under severe shift on narrow tasks, because the model has learned a kind of spurious epistemic smoothness — it interpolates confidently across domains it has seen in aggregate but never deeply. What an expert is ultimately tracking is whether the model's uncertainty representation is semantic (tied to genuine knowledge boundaries) or merely statistical (an artifact of frequency patterns in pre-training data).

The cleanest alternative is conditional calibration evaluated within strata defined by input density under the training distribution — concretely, you bin test examples by their estimated likelihood under a training-distribution model (e.g., a language model perplexity score or a normalizing flow), then compute calibration error within each bin separately rather than aggregating across all test inputs. This separates the two failure modes: a model can be miscalibrated because its softmax outputs are poorly shaped (a model defect, fixable with temperature scaling or Platt scaling) versus because it encounters inputs structurally unlike anything in training (a coverage defect, not fixable by post-hoc recalibration). The distinction matters acutely for the pre-training mixture hypothesis because if you aggregate ECE and find "the high-entropy mixture is better calibrated," you cannot tell whether that's because diverse pre-training actually teaches better uncertainty or merely because the high-entropy model assigns lower density to OOD inputs — producing abstention-like behavior that looks like calibration but is just confident ignorance smoothed over. Concretely, Ovadia et al. (2019, "Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty?") showed that under dataset shift, deep ensembles maintained better calibration than single models, but this advantage collapsed when shift severity was high — exactly the regime where the density-stratified view would have flagged coverage gaps rather than model miscalibration. A sharper tool still is selective calibration (Geifman & El-Yaniv's framework), which asks: for the subset of inputs where the model chooses to be confident, is it actually accurate? — this directly probes whether high-entropy pre-training produces genuine selective competence or merely diffuse overconfidence. If you find that the high-entropy model has worse selective calibration on narrow tasks despite better aggregate ECE, that's the smoking gun that the pre-training diversity is buying statistical smoothness, not semantic uncertainty.

Temperature scaling finds a scalar T that minimizes NLL on a validation set by softening (T>1) or sharpening (T<1) the entire logit distribution uniformly — but OOD inputs are typically overconfident, so tuning T on an OOD validation set pushes T above 1, which then also softens predictions on in-distribution inputs that were already well-calibrated or even underconfident. The in-distribution tail is the precise region where this hurts most: low-frequency, hard in-distribution examples (e.g., rare syntactic constructions, minority-class inputs) often already have diffuse, uncertain logit distributions, and applying T>1 spreads them further, producing underconfidence on exactly the inputs where the model's hesitation was correct and meaningful. Concretely, Guo et al. (2017, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks") demonstrated temperature scaling works well when val and test come from the same distribution, but the method assumes the miscalibration direction is uniform — an assumption that breaks immediately under shift. Kumar et al. (2019, "Verified Uncertainty Calibration") quantified this: when the calibration set is even moderately shifted, temperature scaling can increase ECE on the original distribution by 2-4 percentage points while appearing to improve aggregate ECE on the shifted set, a hidden regression invisible without stratified evaluation. The mechanism is a form of calibration budget misallocation — you're spending your one degree of freedom (T) to fix OOD overconfidence, and the cost is paid by the in-distribution tail where the model's native uncertainty was its most reliable signal. For LLMs specifically, this pathology is severe because the in-distribution tail often contains the highest-stakes inputs: ambiguous queries, knowledge-boundary cases, and novel compositions — precisely where you want the model's raw uncertainty preserved rather than diluted.

The direction is overconfidence on wrong answers — not overconfidence in general, but specifically the model assigns high probability to an incorrect deterministic output because it has learned to mimic the distributional behavior of web text, where multiple plausible continuations are genuinely valid, and it incorrectly applies that same soft probability spreading to domains where only one continuation is correct. The mechanistic reason is that next-token cross-entropy loss is minimized by outputting the true conditional distribution P(next token | context) — on web text, this distribution is genuinely diffuse (many valid continuations), so the model learns to place moderate probability mass across several tokens, which is correct for web text but pathological for arithmetic, where the target distribution is a delta function. When the model encounters "247 × 13 =", the correct training signal would concentrate all mass on "3211", but because the model has internalized a prior toward soft distributions from its dominant training regime, it spreads mass across plausible-looking numbers — and crucially, the mode of that spread is often confidently wrong rather than uniformly uncertain, because the model pattern-matches to surface features of similar-looking web text problems. Srivastava et al. (BIG-Bench, 2022) documented this concretely: models showed higher confidence on arithmetic and formal reasoning tasks than on open-ended tasks, yet accuracy was lower, producing a characteristic overconfidence signature specifically on structured tasks that worsened with scale before instruction tuning corrected it. The deeper issue is that the model cannot distinguish "I am uncertain because multiple answers are valid" from "I am uncertain because I don't know the answer" — both get represented as diffuse logits, but the former is epistemically appropriate while the latter is miscalibration, and web-text pretraining provides almost no gradient signal to learn that distinction for deterministic domains.

The core mechanism is that RLHF optimizes for human preference over outputs, and human raters systematically prefer confident, fluent, decisive answers over hedged ones — so the reward model learns to score confident responses higher independent of their correctness, which then drives the policy model to sharpen its output distributions as a reward-maximizing strategy rather than as a reflection of genuine certainty. This is a direct gradient conflict: the pre-training objective pushes toward calibrated uncertainty (matching the true conditional distribution), while the RL objective pushes toward expressed confidence as a stylistic property, and on deterministic tasks where the pre-training model was already overconfident, RLHF amplifies that overconfidence because confident wrong answers on structured tasks are often fluent and human-preferred over uncertain correct ones. Openai's InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) noted calibration degradation post-RLHF, and Kadavath et al. (2022, "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know") found that while base models showed rough calibration on self-evaluation tasks, RLHF models were measurably overconfident in the 80-95% confidence range — precisely the range corresponding to deterministic tasks where the model is wrong but fluently certain. The most promising intervention is calibration-aware reward modeling: rather than training the reward model purely on preference rankings, augmenting it with a calibration signal — penalizing the policy when its stated confidence on a verifiable task exceeds its empirical accuracy on a held-out batch — essentially adding an ECE term to the RL objective. Concretely, Zhao et al. (2023, "Calibrating Sequence Likelihood") and work on process reward models (Lightman et al., 2023) suggest that rewarding reasoning traces rather than final answers partially recovers calibration because it forces the model to expose intermediate uncertainty rather than just optimizing terminal output confidence. The key insight is that calibration and alignment are only in conflict when the reward model is blind to correctness — if you can ground the reward signal in verifiable outcomes (code execution, formal proof checking, arithmetic verification), you can align expressed confidence with actual accuracy without sacrificing instruction-following gains.

The miscalibration a PRM inherits is fluency-validity conflation: human annotators cannot distinguish "this step follows logically" from "this step reads as if it follows logically," so the PRM is trained to reward surface coherence — correct syntax, plausible variable reuse, familiar proof moves — rather than semantic validity, producing a reward signal that is well-calibrated on easy steps and systematically overestimates correctness on subtly invalid steps that are linguistically indistinguishable from valid ones. Lightman et al. (2023, "Let's Verify Step by Step") trained their PRM800K dataset with human annotators on GSM8K and MATH — but MATH competition problems were specifically chosen because humans can verify individual algebraic steps, which flatters the approach; the real failure mode appears when steps involve non-obvious lemma applications or integer overflow cases where the annotation interface shows a plausible-looking equation and the annotator marks it correct because the numbers look right. This interacts catastrophically with deterministic-task overconfidence: the base model already assigns high confidence to fluent wrong answers, and now the PRM also assigns high step-level scores to those same fluent wrong steps, so the combined system — policy model scored by PRM — has two compounding overconfidence signals both rooted in the same surface-fluency prior from web-text pretraining, with no corrective gradient anywhere in the pipeline. The result is a specific failure signature Lightman et al. observed but underemphasized: PRM-guided search finds solutions that are locally coherent at every step but globally wrong, because the search is optimizing a reward that cannot detect the class of errors where each step is plausible conditioned on the previous one but the chain as a whole drifts from the correct solution path. A concrete intervention is automated step verification via symbolic execution or unit testing where possible (as in AlphaCode 2's filtered sampling), which replaces human fluency judgment with ground-truth correctness signals — but this is only tractable for tasks with executable semantics, leaving formal prose reasoning, legal logic, and scientific inference entirely unaddressed. The deeper structural problem is that PRM miscalibration is invisible in aggregate metrics: if your eval is final-answer accuracy, a PRM that rewards fluent-but-wrong steps can still improve pass@1 by pruning obviously incoherent chains, masking the fact that it is systematically overconfident on the most dangerous error class — subtle, confident, fluent incorrectness.

The relationship is not monotonic — there is a threshold effect, but it operates through a specific mechanism: at low N, best-of-N sampling under a miscalibrated PRM worsens calibration because you are efficiently selecting the most fluently-wrong solution from a small pool, but at sufficiently large N, the correct solution appears in the candidate set with high probability (since the base model does have nonzero probability on correct answers), and if the PRM can distinguish correct final answers even when it cannot verify intermediate steps, selection flips toward correct solutions. Lightman et al. (2023) showed this inflection empirically on MATH: PRM-guided best-of-N improved faster than ORM-guided best-of-N as N scaled, but both showed diminishing returns past N≈100, suggesting the recoverable calibration gain is bounded by the base model's coverage of correct solutions — once the correct answer is reliably in the candidate pool, further scaling just re-selects it, and the PRM's step-level miscalibration becomes irrelevant to final accuracy while remaining latent in the confidence scores. The threshold mechanism that actually recovers calibration rather than just accuracy is diversity-forced search: if you explicitly penalize candidate similarity (as in diverse beam search or temperature-elevated sampling), you force the search to explore structurally different solution paths rather than N variations of the same fluent-wrong approach, increasing the probability that at least one path reaches the correct answer through a genuinely valid route that the PRM then scores highly. Snell et al. (2024, "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute") formalized this, showing that compute scaling via sampling with a verifier outperforms beam search specifically because beam search's left-to-right commitment collapses solution diversity early, trapping search in the basin of fluent-but-wrong local optima — the calibration recovery requires breadth before depth. The residual danger is that confidence scores remain miscalibrated even when final answers are correct: the model arrives at the right answer through a chain the PRM scores highly, but neither the policy's token probabilities nor the PRM's step scores reflect genuine logical certainty — they reflect fluency selection pressure, so any downstream system consuming confidence scores rather than just final answers inherits the full miscalibration despite the accuracy improvement.

When two structurally different paths reach different final answers with similar PRM scores, the system is in a calibration collapse state: the PRM's score is no longer informative about correctness, so any adjudication method that relies on PRM scores is essentially random with respect to truth, yet the expressed confidence remains high because both paths are fluent — the system confidently disagrees with itself while having no internal signal that distinguishes which answer is correct. The correct interpretation of this state is that the PRM score spread across competing answers is the most honest uncertainty signal available: if answer A has aggregate PRM score 0.81 and answer B has 0.79 across diverse paths, the system should report ~50% confidence on both, not pick A at 81% confidence — but current systems almost universally take the argmax and report it with the winner's score, converting a genuine uncertainty signal into false precision. Wang et al. (2023, "Self-Consistency Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning") showed that majority voting across diverse sampled paths outperforms single-path greedy decoding precisely because answer frequency across structurally independent paths is a better calibration proxy than any single path's internal score — when two answers split the vote roughly evenly, self-consistency implicitly flags uncertainty, which is epistemically correct behavior even though the method was designed for accuracy not calibration. The adjudication mechanism that most honestly handles this without ground truth is answer-conditioned path auditing: for each candidate final answer, collect all paths that reached it, compute the variance of PRM scores across those paths, and treat high variance as a signal of fragile justification — a correct answer reached by multiple structurally independent high-scoring paths is more trustworthy than one reached by a single fluent path, even if the single path scores higher in absolute terms. Concretely, this is a form of epistemic triangulation: you are asking not "which answer has the best justification" but "which answer is robust to changes in justification approach," which is a much stronger criterion for deterministic tasks where correctness is path-independent. The residual unsolved problem is that this entire framework breaks when the correct answer is systematically underrepresented in the base model's distribution — if web-text pretraining has made certain wrong answers fluent attractors, diversity-forced search may generate many structurally different paths that all converge on the same fluent-wrong answer, producing false consensus that self-consistency and path auditing cannot distinguish from genuine agreement.
